title: What Is the Best Air Filter for My HVAC System?
h1: What Type of Air Filter Is Best for Your HVAC System?
description: For most homes, a MERV 8 to 13 pleated filter that fits snugly is the best HVAC filter. Learn how MERV works, when to upgrade and how often to change filters.
quick_answer: For most homes, the best HVAC filter is a pleated filter rated MERV 8 to 13 that fits the slot snugly. MERV 8 catches common dust and pollen. MERV 11 to 13 catches finer particles like smoke and pet dander, but only if your system has enough airflow to handle it. A thicker media filter makes higher ratings easier on your system.
body:
Filters matter more than most people think. They protect your blower, coil and ducts from dust, and they help keep the air in your home cleaner. But the "best" filter isn't always the one with the highest rating. It's the one that cleans well without choking your system's airflow.

What does MERV mean?

MERV stands for Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value. It rates how well a filter captures particles of different sizes, on a scale from 1 to 16 for most residential and commercial filters.

  • MERV 1 to 4: Basic fiberglass filters. They protect the equipment from large debris but do little for air quality.
  • MERV 5 to 8: Pleated filters that catch dust, pollen, lint and mold spores. A good baseline for most homes.
  • MERV 9 to 12: Better at catching fine dust, pet dander and some smoke particles.
  • MERV 13: Captures a large share of fine particles, including much of the smoke that comes with wildfires. A strong choice if your system can handle it.
  • MERV 14 to 16: Usually used in commercial and medical settings. Most home systems aren't designed for them.

Some retailers use their own rating systems. Look for the MERV number on the package so you can compare apples to apples.

Can a filter be too restrictive?

Yes. A higher MERV filter has denser material, which means more resistance to airflow. If your system wasn't designed for it, you can end up with:

  • Weaker airflow at the registers
  • A frozen AC coil in summer
  • A furnace that overheats and shuts off on its safety switch
  • Higher energy use and more strain on the blower motor

Thin 1-inch filters at MERV 13 are the most likely to cause trouble. A 4-inch or 5-inch media filter cabinet has much more surface area, so it can filter finely with less restriction. If you want better filtration, adding a media cabinet is often the best upgrade.

Which filter is right for your home?

  • Typical household: MERV 8 pleated filter, changed regularly.
  • Pets or allergies: MERV 11 to 13, ideally in a thicker media cabinet.
  • Wildfire smoke concerns: MERV 13 during smoke events, if the system can handle it. Keep windows closed and run the fan.
  • Older system with weak airflow: Stay around MERV 8 and have a technician check the ducts and blower before upgrading.

Electrostatic and washable filters exist, but in our experience they're harder to keep clean and often don't perform as well as a fresh pleated filter.

How often should you change your filter?

It depends on the filter's thickness and your home. As a general guide:

  • 1-inch filters: every 1 to 3 months
  • 4-inch or 5-inch media filters: every 6 to 12 months
  • More often if you have pets, allergies, construction going on or heavy smoke outside

The easiest rule is to check it monthly. If it looks gray and clogged, change it. After Santa Ana winds or a smoky week, check it right away.

Does the filter fit properly?

A great filter that doesn't fit is a bad filter. Gaps around the edges let air bypass the filter completely. Make sure:

  1. The size printed on the filter matches the slot exactly.
  2. The airflow arrow points toward the furnace or air handler.
  3. The filter door or grille closes fully.
  4. There are no gaps between the filter and the frame.

In many local homes, the filter is in a return grille in a hallway ceiling or wall rather than at the furnace in the attic. Some homes have more than one, so check all your returns.

What if a filter isn't enough?

If you still have dust, allergy or smoke problems with a good filter in place, look at the rest of the system. Leaky return ducts in the attic or garage can pull in unfiltered air. Our indoor air quality team can add a media filter cabinet, air purifier or UV light, and check your ducts for leaks that bypass the filter.
faqs: Is a HEPA filter good for a home HVAC system?

True HEPA filters are too restrictive for most residential HVAC systems. They're usually used in portable air purifiers or in whole-home units with their own fan. A MERV 13 media filter is a more practical choice for most central systems.
Does a more expensive filter save money?
Not always. A pricey filter that restricts airflow can make your system work harder. The best value is usually a mid-range pleated filter that fits well and gets changed on schedule.
Can a dirty filter damage my system?
Yes. A clogged filter cuts airflow, which can freeze the AC coil, overheat the furnace and wear out the blower motor. It's one of the most common causes of service calls we see.
